preserved_analysis.summary: Recent public allegations, incident-monitor entries, and research concerning model and dataset distillation raise an emerging governance question: when a downstream system materially inherits capability from an upstream model or corpus, computational transformation may obscure the derivation chain without extinguishing the upstream contribution. Current debate is often framed as copyright or model theft, but the deeper issue is whether attribution, licensing, safety, constitutional, regulatory, audit, and evidence obligations persist through successive transformations of learned capability.
preserved_analysis.why_it_matters_to_CAM: Repeated distillation can preserve useful capability while progressively weakening visible lineage. If transformation alone is treated as extinguishing provenance, downstream developers may retain the benefit of upstream human works, safety controls, governance design, or model behaviour while avoiding corresponding attribution, accountability, audit, or legal obligations. A candidate CAM principle is: derived intelligence carries derived provenance obligations. This is an emerging governance proposition, not a concluded legal rule or confirmed failure mode.

possible_taxonomy_mapping.mapping_note: Possible future mapping to provenance collapse, attribution loss, governance-lineage discontinuity, and audit-surface degradation. No new failure mode is recommended at this stage.

preserved_analysis.next_action: Monitor litigation, regulation, technical provenance methods, model-supply-chain disclosures, and documented distillation campaigns. Before creating a CAM proposal, distinguish training provenance, model distillation, capability inheritance, attribution inheritance, governance inheritance, safety provenance, constitutional provenance, and legal inheritance. Evaluate the candidate principle: derived intelligence carries derived provenance obligations.
